families.name: Damselfishes
cues: Tail from deeply forked to rounded
Most common family in IMR surveys

juv.note: Dascyllus juveniles: black with white blotches, still clearly Dascyllus. Chromis and Pomacentrus: no juvenile source found.

marks: Deep, flattened body with a small mouth
Colours vary between individuals and between places for the same species
life: Many are territorial; they eat algae, small animals or plankton
Males guard the eggs, laid on the bottom
Anemonefishes (Amphiprion) live with large sea anemones
Most are small, at most about 35 cm

families.name: Butterflyfishes
cues: Small terminal mouth: feeds on coral polyps
Dorsal, tail and anal fins curve into a disc
look: Angelfish: spine on the gill cover, iridescent blue

lsrc.f:Angelfishes: IMR fish presentation, slide 10 and Pierre, 2026-11-06

juv.note: Same disc shape; some Chaetodon juveniles add a rear dorsal black spot.

marks: Very flat, deep body; small mouth at the tip of the snout, with brush-like teeth
Scales run onto the dorsal and anal fins
Many have a dark band through the eye and an eyespot towards the back
life: Most live in male-female pairs, active by day near coral reefs
Many eat coral polyps, small invertebrates and algae; some eat plankton

families.name: Angelfishes
cues: Oval like a butterflyfish, continuous dorsal fin
Spine on the gill cover (opercular spine)
look: Butterflyfish: no opercular spine, no iridescent blue

lsrc.f:Butterflyfishes: IMR fish presentation, slide 11 and Pierre, 2026-11-06

phase: Juveniles look very different from adults

juv.note: Pomacanthus juveniles: striking patterns unlike the adults (e.g. dark blue with electric blue and white rings). Centropyge: no juvenile source found.

marks: The gill-cover spine sits at the corner of its front bone (the preopercle), on the cheek
Many have a trailing tip at the back of the dorsal and anal fins
Tail rounded to deeply crescent-shaped
life: Mostly shallower than 20 m, rarely below 50 m, near coral reefs
Pairs or harems; many change sex from female to male
Centropyge eat mostly algae, Genicanthus plankton, most others sponges and invertebrates

families.name: Spadefishes
cues: Black band over the eye in adults
phase: Juvenile and adult colours can differ completely
The juvenile pinnate spadefish mimics a toxic flatworm

marks: Deep body, very flat from the side, with a small mouth
life: Eat algae and small invertebrates

families.name: Moorish Idol
cues: Only one species in the family
Yellow on the body and a yellow saddle
look: Bannerfish: no yellow on the saddle

juv.note: No source compares juvenile and adult colour; the horns are an adult feature.

marks: Disc-shaped, very flat body; long tube-like snout with a small mouth
Dorsal spines drawn out into a long whip-like filament

life: Common on coral reefs; eats mainly sponges and other bottom invertebrates

apart.f:Surgeonfishes: Surgeonfish: a spine on the tail base, no long dorsal filament

families.name: Surgeonfishes
cues: Scalpel on the tail base (caudal peduncle)
Moderate fishing vulnerability in the Philippines

One long dorsal fin without a notch
Very small scales

apart.f:MoorishIdol: Moorish Idol: no spine on the tail base, long whip-like dorsal filament
apart.f:Rabbitfishes: Rabbitfish: no spine on the tail base, a spine at each end of the pelvic fins

families.name: Rabbitfishes
cues: Slightly elongated mouth with puckered lips

juv.note: Juveniles look similar to the adults (Siganus puellus); same body plan.

marks: Each pelvic fin has a spine at both ends, with 3 soft rays between
13 strong dorsal spines, venomous

Some swim in schools, others stay among corals; up to about 40 cm

apart.f:Surgeonfishes: Surgeonfish: a spine on the tail base, eye high on the head

families.name: Wrasses
cues: Swims with the pectoral fins, flapping like a bird

marks: Cylindrical body; fins without spines

families.name: Sandperches
look: Lizardfish: sits arched, triangular mouth with teeth
marks: Pelvic fins set under or in front of the pectoral fins
Dorsal fin with 4-5 spines and a long soft part
life: Eat small bottom invertebrates and fish
Territorial; a male with several females

families.name: Barracudas
marks: Long, slender silver body with a pointed head and a jutting lower jaw lined with fangs
Two small dorsal fins set far apart, the second above the anal fin; forked tail

families.name: Trumpetfishes
marks: Long, stiff body and a tube-like snout with a small barbel under the chin
A row of separate small spines along the back; rounded tail with no filament (the cornetfish has one)
Often hangs head-down or swims close against a larger fish; yellow or grey-brown

families.name: Shrimpfishes
marks: Razor-thin body in clear bony plates, ending in a long spine at the back
Groups move together head-down, in perfect step, and hide among sea urchin spines

families.name: Sweepers
marks: Deep, side-flattened body tapering towards the tail, with a very large eye
One short dorsal fin set forward on the back
Dense schools in caves and under ledges by day

families.name: Frogfishes
families.why: Dauin muck-diving icon
marks: Globe-shaped, lumpy body and an enormous mouth that opens upward; no scales, the skin often with flaps or warts
A 'fishing rod' spine on the snout, tipped with a lure
Colour very variable; many look like a sponge or a clump of algae

families.name: Ghost Pipefishes
families.why: Dauin muck-diving icon
marks: Short body in star-shaped bony plates, with a tube snout and large, fan-like fins
Large pelvic fins under the body (pipefishes and seahorses have none); the female's form a pouch for the eggs
Drifts head-down beside what it imitates in shape and colour: algae, a seafan or a feather star

families.name: Seahorses
marks: Head bent at a right angle to the body, like a horse's head
Curling, gripping tail with no tail fin, wrapped around seagrass, coral or a seafan
Upright body in bony rings, moved by a small fin on the back

families.name: Pipefishes
families.why: seahorses, pygmy seahorses, pipefishes, pipehorses
marks: Long, thin, stiff body in bony rings, with a tube snout and a tiny mouth
Head in line with the body, not bent at a right angle as in seahorses
No pelvic fins, unlike the ghost pipefishes

families.name: Dragonets
families.why: mandarinfish and fingered dragonets
marks: Small, low fish shuffling or 'walking' over sand, rubble or silty bottoms
Often vividly patterned; males have longer, filament-like first dorsal spines

families.name: Sea Moths
families.why: Pegasus seamoths on the sand
marks: Small, flat body in a box of bony plates, with a long flat snout and the mouth underneath
Large, wing-like pectoral fins spread flat to the sides
'Walks' over the bottom on thin pelvic fins; coloured like shell or rubble

families.name: Scorpionfishes
families.why: scorpionfishes and Rhinopias (lionfishes are the IMR Lionfish entry)
marks: Stocky, with a big head full of bony ridges, spines and skin flaps
Lies still on the bottom, mottled red, brown and white to match it
Leaf scorpionfish: a flat, leaf-like body with a high dorsal fin, rocking with the surge

families.name: Stonefishes
families.why: stonefishes, devilfishes, cockatoo waspfish
marks: Lumpy, warty skin without scales: looks like a rock or a lump of algae
Sits still, sometimes half-buried in sand with only the upturned mouth and the eyes showing

families.name: Waspfishes
marks: Side-flattened body with a tall dorsal fin starting above the eye, like a crest
Mottled brown, cream or reddish; sways from side to side like a dead leaf in the surge

families.name: Flying Gurnards
families.why: muck-diving classic
marks: Huge pectoral fins spread like wings, with spots and wavy blue lines
Blunt, box-like head and body in bony armour

families.name: Stargazers
families.why: buried in the sand
marks: Big, box-like head with the eyes on top, looking up
Large mouth opening straight upward, often with fringed lips

families.name: Jawfishes
families.why: burrows in the sand
marks: Big head with large eyes and a huge mouth, poking out of a burrow in sand or rubble
A male may hold a ball of eggs in his mouth

families.name: Snake Eels
families.why: heads out of the sand
marks: Round, snake-like body, usually buried in sand with only the head out
Many have small pectoral fins behind the head (morays have none)
Harlequin snake eel: pale with broad dark rings all the way round the body

families.name: Morays
families.why: morays and ribbon eels
marks: Thick, scaleless eel with one long fin over the back, round the tail and under the belly; no pectoral fins
Usually only the head shows, out of a hole or crevice
A small round gill opening on the side of the head; many show fang-like teeth

families.name: Garden Eels
families.why: spotted and spaghetti garden eels on the sand slopes
marks: Very thin eels in colonies, standing half out of burrows in sand and swaying in the current; they sink back in when approached

families.name: Stingrays
families.why: stingrays on the sand
marks: Flat, round to oval disc, the head part of it, lying on the bottom
Tail armed with one or several venomous spines, and no tail fin

families.name: Requiem Sharks
families.why: reef sharks
marks: Five gill slits on each side, the last one above the base of the pectoral fin; round eyes
Blacktip reef shark: black tip on the first dorsal fin; whitetip reef shark: white tips on the first dorsal and upper tail

families.name: Porcupinefishes
families.why: porcupinefishes and burrfishes
marks: Body covered in sharp spines, unlike the smooth pufferfishes
Puffs itself up into a spiny ball when alarmed
Beak-like mouth: one fused tooth plate in each jaw

families.name: Jacks
families.why: schools of jacks and trevallies
marks: Side-flattened body, often silvery, with a deeply forked tail on a very thin tail base
Many have a row of hard, ridged scales (scutes) along the rear of the side
Fast swimmers in open water over the reef, often in schools

families.name: Whale Sharks
families.note: A wink, not ID training: unmistakable and fun to meet (whale shark trips from Dauin).

wink.wrong: Bold choice. It's a whale shark, the biggest fish in the sea.

marks: Enormous shark with a broad, flat head and a very wide mouth at the very front of the snout
Dark back with a checkerboard of pale spots and thin pale stripes

families.name: Thresher sharks
families.note: A wink, not ID training: unmistakable and fun to meet (pelagic thresher, Malapascua).

choices: Moorish idol (banner on the wrong end)
wink.right: Correct. That tail was a strong hint.
wink.wrong: Brave. It's a pelagic thresher: the tail is half the shark.

marks: The tail's upper lobe is huge: close to half the shark's whole length

families.name: Hawkfishes
families.why: Pierre's pick after the search of every species confirmed near Dauin (Q216)
marks: Perches on coral heads or sponges, propped on its thick lower pectoral fin rays
Each dorsal fin spine ends in a small tuft
Many are red-spotted or barred on a pale body

families.name: Blennies
families.why: Pierre's pick after the search of every species confirmed near Dauin (Q216)
marks: Blunt, rounded head with the eyes high up, often with small tentacles above the eyes
One long dorsal fin and no scales (gobies have two dorsal fins)
Some copy other fish: the false cleanerfish looks like the cleaner wrasse, but its mouth is under the snout

families.name: Eel-tailed Catfishes
families.why: Pierre's pick after the search of every species confirmed near Dauin (Q216)
marks: Eel-like tail: the rear dorsal, tail and anal fins joined in one
Four pairs of whisker-like barbels around the mouth
Striped catfish: dark with two thin pale stripes; the young swarm in a tight ball

families.name: Bigeyes
families.why: Pierre's pick after the search of every species confirmed near Dauin (Q216)
marks: Huge eyes; the mouth slants up, the lower jaw sticking out past the upper
Deep, side-flattened body, usually red, able to turn silvery or blotched in moments
Hovers still under ledges or in caves by day

families.name: Tunas & Mackerels
families.why: Pierre's pick after the search of every species confirmed near Dauin (Q216)
marks: Torpedo-shaped body, pointed snout and a deeply forked tail
A row of small finlets behind the second dorsal fin and the anal fin

families.name: Soles
families.why: Pierre's pick after the search of every species confirmed near Dauin (Q216)
marks: Flat body lying on one side, both eyes on the same side of the head
The dorsal fin starts on the head and runs along the edge, the anal fin along the other edge

families.name: Cornetfishes
families.why: Pierre's pick after the search of every species confirmed near Dauin (Q216)
marks: Very long, thin body with a long tube-like snout
Forked tail with a long whip-like filament in the middle (trumpetfishes have none)
Smooth back without a row of spines; often blue lines or spots

families.name: Remoras
families.why: Pierre's pick after the search of every species confirmed near Dauin (Q216)
marks: A flat, oval sucking disc with cross ridges on top of the head
Long, slim body with a broad dark stripe along the side
Rides attached to sharks, rays, turtles or large fish

families.name: Needlefishes
families.why: Pierre's pick after the search of every species confirmed near Dauin (Q216)
marks: Very long, thin body with both jaws drawn out into a narrow beak of sharp teeth
One dorsal fin and the anal fin set far back, near the tail
Swims just under the surface; green or blue back and silvery sides

families.name: Dartfishes
families.why: Pierre's pick (Q217): the dartfishes, a key label of their own
marks: Slim, side-flattened, goby-like body with a long second dorsal fin matching the anal fin below
Hovers above the bottom, usually in pairs, and darts off when approached

families.name: Dottybacks
families.why: Pierre's pick after the search of every species confirmed near Dauin (Q216)
marks: Small, slim fish with one long dorsal fin, staying close to coral, rubble or crevices
Often bright: the magenta dottyback all magenta; the firetail dottyback with a red eye

families.name: Convict Blennies
families.why: Pierre's pick after the search of every species confirmed near Dauin (Q216)
marks: Long, eel-like body with one fin along the back, round the tail and under the belly
The young are black with a white stripe and swim in tight schools by ledges and coral heads, looking like striped catfish

families.name: Triplefins
families.why: Pierre's pick after the search of every species confirmed near Dauin (Q216)
marks: Three separate dorsal fins, two spiny and one soft (blennies have one, gobies two)
Tiny, slim, scaled fish perched on rock or coral

families.name: Gobies
families.why: Pierre, 2026-11-08: the gobies are in circle 3 (the dartfishes have their own key label; the wormfishes are not decided)
marks: Small, with two separate dorsal fins
Pelvic fins fused into a sucker-like cup under the chest
Many, the shrimpgobies, share a burrow with a shrimp
